scenes.title: Can one boundary change a mass?
scenes.text: Watch the blue profile. Changing just one boundary makes it bend, and its lowest eigenvalue rises. Why? Let us build the explanation, then check the same effect in the laboratory.

scenes.title: Start with a flat profile
scenes.text: The horizontal coordinate is position along an extra dimension. The vertical coordinate is field amplitude, not a particle trajectory. With zero slope required at both ends, a constant profile is allowed. Its curvature, and its normal eigenvalue, are zero.

scenes.title: Change the rule at the right edge
scenes.text: Now turn on the boundary coupling, called a. The right edge requires slope plus a times amplitude to equal zero. Our nonzero constant has zero slope but nonzero amplitude. Watch the residual turn red. This profile no longer satisfies the boundary condition.

scenes.title: Find a shape that obeys the rule
scenes.text: We keep zero slope at the left edge. The bulk equation then gives a cosine profile. Change its frequency, x, and watch the right endpoint. Most frequencies still fail. Only the frequency that balances slope against boundary amplitude is allowed.

scenes.title: See the cancellation at the endpoint
scenes.text: For a cosine, the endpoint slope is minus x sine x. The boundary term is a cosine x. At coupling one, these two contributions cancel. Rearranging gives x tangent x equals a. This equation comes directly from the endpoint balance.

scenes.title: From an allowed shape to a spectral gap
scenes.text: Increase the coupling. The allowed profile bends more, while the first root rises. The small graph tracks the same calculation. With interval length pi R, the scaled normal mass is x over pi. It approaches one half as the coupling grows.

scenes.title: Check the prediction in GHU Lab
scenes.text: Now the actual laboratory. We change the boundary strength from zero to four. Watch the paired curve lift above the unpaired curve. At Wilson angle zero, its intercept is exactly the normal gap we just derived. The highlighted input and the plotted result change together.

scenes.title: The reason, in three steps
scenes.text: The boundary rule changed. The constant profile became inadmissible. The lowest allowed mode now has a positive eigenvalue. That is the mechanism behind this gap, in this stated interval problem. The laboratory computes the effect; the boundary argument explains why it happens.
